title: Real Production
description: Deploying against a real backend — endpoints, headers, and what the frontend is not responsible for.
---

# Deploying to production

A production build contains no MSW, no demo state and no seeded account. It
talks to your backend and nothing else. Everything below assumes you have one.

## Environment variables

```bash
VUESTRATA_RUNTIME_MODE=production
VUESTRATA_USE_MOCKS=false
VUESTRATA_AUTH_ADAPTER=jwt            # or oauth, which needs SESSION_PERSISTENCE=none
VUESTRATA_SESSION_PERSISTENCE=refresh-cookie   # the default; none | session | local
VUESTRATA_API_URL=https://api.yourcompany.com
VUESTRATA_APP_TITLE=Acme Console
VUESTRATA_RELEASE=$GIT_SHA            # optional, for error reports
```

The build rejects a placeholder `API_URL`, a `mock` adapter, `USE_MOCKS=true`,
and `oauth` with any `SESSION_PERSISTENCE` but `none`. Those are not hints —
they fail the build. Because the production default is `refresh-cookie`, an
`oauth` build has to set `none` explicitly. What each persistence mode needs
from your backend is in [Environment](../6.configuration/1.environment).

Every one of these values is inlined into the bundle at build time. The first
three stop there: they decide what is in the bundle. The other four are
defaults, which a deployment may replace when the app starts — so one build can
serve staging and production alike. [Build once, deploy many](#build-once-deploy-many)
shows how, and [Environment](../6.configuration/1.environment#build-time-and-start-time)
has the exact rule.

Serve the API over `https://` when the app is. A browser blocks an `http://`
API called from an `https://` page as mixed content, whatever the CSP allows,
and the build cannot check for it: it does not know how the app will be served.

## The endpoint contract

Your backend must implement these. The frontend calls them through `apiFetch`,
so the base URL, credentials mode and CSRF handling are applied uniformly.

### Both adapters

| Method | Path           | Body | Returns |
| ------ | -------------- | ---- | ------- |
| `POST` | `/auth/logout` | —    | `204`   |
| `GET`  | `/auth/me`     | —    | `User`  |

### `jwt` adapter only

| Method | Path                      | Body                                            | Returns                                    |
| ------ | ------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| `POST` | `/auth/login`             | `{ email, password }`                           | `{ user, token, refreshToken, expiresIn }` |
| `POST` | `/auth/register`          | `{ email, password, name }`                     | same as login                              |
| `POST` | `/auth/refresh`           | `{ refreshToken }`; none under `refresh-cookie` | `{ token, refreshToken, expiresIn }`       |
| `POST` | `/auth/magic-link`        | `{ email }`                                     | `{ message }`                              |
| `POST` | `/auth/magic-link/verify` | `{ token }`                                     | login response                             |
| `POST` | `/auth/mfa/setup`         | —                                               | `{ secret, qrCodeUrl, backupCodes }`       |
| `POST` | `/auth/mfa/verify`        | `{ mfaToken, code }`                            | login response                             |
| `POST` | `/auth/mfa/disable`       | —                                               | any `2xx`; the body is not read            |

`/auth/login` may answer `{ mfaRequired: true, mfaToken }` instead of a session.
The app then shows the code prompt and posts that `mfaToken` with the user's
code to `/auth/mfa/verify`.

`/auth/refresh` returns no `user`; after a reload the app loads it from
`GET /auth/me` with the new token. Under `refresh-cookie`, the default, the
refresh token is an HttpOnly cookie instead of a body field: the backend sets it
on every response that starts a session and reads it on `/auth/refresh` and
`/auth/logout`. The app sends `credentials: 'include'` on its `/auth/*` requests
for exactly that, which needs credentialed CORS when the API is on another
origin.
[What `refresh-cookie` needs from the backend](../6.configuration/1.environment#what-refresh-cookie-needs-from-the-backend)
has the full list.

### `oauth` adapter only

| Method | Path              | Body                                                                                                 | Returns                                     |
| ------ | ----------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
| `GET`  | `/auth/authorize` | query: `response_type=code`, `state`, `code_challenge`, `code_challenge_method=S256`, `redirect_uri` | `302` to the identity provider              |
| `GET`  | `/auth/:provider` | the same query; `:provider` is `google`, `github` or `microsoft`                                     | `302` to that provider                      |
| `POST` | `/auth/token`     | `{ grant_type: 'authorization_code', code, code_verifier, redirect_uri }`                            | login response, with the session cookie set |

The two `GET` routes are browser navigations, not API calls. The provider's
redirect must end at `redirect_uri` — the app's own `/auth/callback` — with
`code` and `state`. The adapter checks `state` against the value it stored
before redirecting and never sends it to the backend; `/auth/token` receives the
PKCE `code_verifier` instead.

A route your backend does not implement should be reflected in the adapter's
`capabilities`, not left to fail at click time. The UI hides controls for
capabilities an adapter does not advertise — that is the whole point of the
capability flags.

### Domain endpoints

Every domain module follows one collection contract:

```
GET    /{resource}?page=&pageSize=&search=&sortBy=&sortOrder=&<filters>
       → { data: T[], meta: { total, page, pageSize, totalPages } }
GET    /{resource}/:id      → T
POST   /{resource}          → T (201)
PATCH  /{resource}/:id      → T
DELETE /{resource}/:id      → 204
```

The zod schema in each module's `types.ts` **is** the contract. Responses are
validated on arrival, so a backend that drifts fails loudly at the boundary
instead of rendering `undefined` three components deep.

## Choosing a transport

`AUTH_ADAPTER` also decides how credentials travel, and the two modes are
mutually exclusive by design:

|                 | `bearer` (jwt)                                        | `cookie`                           |
| --------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------- |
| `credentials`   | `omit`; `include` on `/auth/*` under `refresh-cookie` | `include`                          |
| `Authorization` | `Bearer <token>`                                      | absent                             |
| CSRF header     | none                                                  | `X-CSRF-Token` on mutating methods |
| Token storage   | memory + refresh call                                 | HttpOnly cookie, unreadable by JS  |

::alert{type="warning"}
Sending both is not "belt and braces" — it is a CSRF hole. A cookie is attached
by the browser automatically, so an endpoint that accepts cookie auth will honour
a cross-site request whether or not the bearer header is present. The template
sends exactly one.
::

**Prefer cookies** for a first-party app: an HttpOnly cookie is not readable by
injected script, and XSS is a far more common failure than CSRF. Use bearer when
the API is on a different origin and you cannot set a cookie for it.

## Security headers

The headers are **generated**, from the defaults in
`scripts/security/headers.mjs` and from what your project adds under `headers`
in `src/modules/app/config/deploy.config.ts`, into every place that serves them:

| Target                                 | Used by                                        |
| -------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- |
| `public/_headers`                      | Netlify-style static hosts                     |
| `vercel.json` → `headers`              | the Vercel demo                                |
| `docker/nginx.conf`, `docker/runtime/` | the Docker image, completed at container start |
| `<meta>` in `index.html`               | a host that sends no headers                   |

Never edit those by hand, nor the comment above the `<meta>`, which is generated
with it. Change `deploy.config.ts` and run `vpr security:headers`. `vpr lint`
fails when any of them has drifted, which is what the four hand-maintained
copies never had.

`headers.mjs` is Vuestrata's file and is replaced by an upgrade. What you need
beyond its defaults goes in `deploy.config.ts`, which is yours.

::alert{type="warning"}
**nginx does not inherit `add_header`.** A block that declares any `add_header`
of its own drops every one inherited from an outer level — so a single
`Cache-Control` inside `location /` silently removes the CSP, HSTS and
frame-options headers from exactly the responses that matter. The generated
config re-`include`s the header snippet in every location for this reason.
::

The CSP is the part worth reading:

```
default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; connect-src 'self'; …
```

### Allowing another origin

Out of the box the app may connect only to its own origin, and to the API when
that is on another one. Almost every real app needs more: an identity provider,
an error tracker, a realtime endpoint, an image host. Declare them:

```ts
// src/modules/app/config/deploy.config.ts
export default defineDeployConfig({
  headers: {
    // Known when you commit.
    connectSrc: ['https://login.yourcompany.com', 'wss://realtime.yourcompany.com'],

    // Different per environment: the origin of a variable's value.
    connectSrcFromEnv: ['VUESTRATA_ERROR_REPORTING_DSN', 'VUESTRATA_SUPABASE_URL'],
    // …and its wss:// twin, for a service that also opens a WebSocket.
    websocketFromEnv: ['VUESTRATA_SUPABASE_URL'],

    imgSrc: ['https://images.yourcompany.com'],
    frameSrc: ['https://js.stripe.com'],
    fontSrc: ['https://fonts.yourcompany.com'],
  },
})
```

Then run `vpr security:headers` and commit what it changed. The drift check
reads the same file, so a policy widened this way passes `vpr lint`.

| Option                    | Adds to           | Accepts                                                            |
| ------------------------- | ----------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `connectSrc`              | `connect-src`     | origins                                                            |
| `connectSrcFromEnv`       | `connect-src`     | names of variables holding a URL                                   |
| `websocketFromEnv`        | `connect-src`     | the same; `https://x` is added as `wss://x`                        |
| `imgSrc`                  | `img-src`         | origins, or `https:`, `data:`, `blob:`                             |
| `frameSrc`                | `frame-src`       | origins                                                            |
| `fontSrc`                 | `font-src`        | origins, or `data:`                                                |
| `frameAncestors`          | `frame-ancestors` | `'self'` or origins; the default is `'none'`                       |
| `crossOriginOpenerPolicy` | the COOP header   | `same-origin` (default), `same-origin-allow-popups`, `unsafe-none` |

Every list adds to the defaults; none can remove a source. `script-src` is not
configurable.

::alert{type="danger"}
**A source is an origin: `scheme://host[:port]`, nothing after it.**
`https://api.yourcompany.com/v1` is not one, and a browser that meets one
invalid source **discards the entire directive**, silently — the policy then
restricts nothing. So the generator refuses anything that is not exactly an
origin, with the origin to write instead. A leading `*.` label is allowed
(`https://*.ingest.sentry.io`); a bare `*` is not. An option it does not know
is refused too, rather than ignored as a typo would be.
::

### Where each origin comes from

`connectSrc` is written into every target as it is. The API origin and the
`…FromEnv` variables are different: their values belong to an environment, so
they are resolved where the environment is known.

- **The Docker image** resolves them when the container starts. The committed
  files under `docker/runtime/` are templates, and the image's entrypoint
  completes them from the container's environment. Nothing about one
  environment is baked into the image.
- **A static host** has no start, so its headers are fixed when it is deployed.
  Run the generator with `--from-env` in the deploy step, before the build:

  ```bash
  VUESTRATA_API_URL=https://api.yourcompany.com \
    node scripts/security/sync-headers.mjs --from-env
  vpr build
  ```

  It writes `public/_headers`, and the CSP `<meta>` of `index.html`, with the
  origin of `VUESTRATA_API_URL` and of every variable named under
  `connectSrcFromEnv` and `websocketFromEnv`. Both are written because a browser
  enforces both: a tag left at `'self'` would block what the header had just
  allowed. **Do not commit the result**: it describes one environment, and
  `--check` would report it as drift. `--api-url=<url>` sets the API URL alone.

- **Vercel** reads `vercel.json` from the repository before the build runs, so
  nothing rendered during the build reaches it. List the origins under
  `connectSrc`, where they are committed.

Without `--from-env` the generator reads nothing from the environment. That is
what makes `vpr lint` give the same answer on every machine.

### Popup sign-in and embedding

`Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin`, the default, cuts `window.opener`
between your app and a window on another origin. Sign-in flows that open a
popup and wait for it to report back depend on that link: MSAL's `loginPopup`
and `acquireTokenPopup`, Firebase's `signInWithPopup`, Google Identity Services.
Under the default they hang or fail with no useful error. Set:

```ts
headers: {
  crossOriginOpenerPolicy: 'same-origin-allow-popups'
}
```

A redirect flow needs nothing; the template's own `oauth` adapter uses one.

The app refuses to be framed (`frame-ancestors 'none'`, `X-Frame-Options:
DENY`). To embed it in a portal, list who may: `frameAncestors: ["'self'"]`
sends `SAMEORIGIN` with it, and a list of other origins drops
`X-Frame-Options`, which has no way to express one.

### The `<meta>` tag, and a host that sends no headers

`index.html` carries a copy of the policy for a host that sends none. It is the
header's policy with one difference: `frame-ancestors` is absent, because a
browser ignores it in a `<meta>`. Everything else is the same, `connect-src`
included: `'self'`, the origins under `connectSrc`, and the API and environment
origins when the generator is run with `--from-env` or `--api-url`.

A browser enforces the tag **in addition to** the header, so the two must name
the same origins. The generator writes both from the same inputs, which is why
`--from-env` rewrites `index.html` as well as `public/_headers`.

On a host that sends no headers, the tag still restricts scripts, styles,
images, frames and connections. What it cannot do is stop another site from
framing the app. Treat a host that cannot send headers as unsupported for
production.

**The Docker image is the exception.** Its API origin is decided when a
container starts, long after `index.html` was written, so no tag could name it.
The image's page therefore reads `connect-src *` and leaves connections to the
header, which that image always sends. The generator writes that form only when
asked:

```bash
node scripts/security/sync-headers.mjs --runtime-config
```

The `Dockerfile` passes the flag, with `--api-url` so that the image also
records the API URL it was built with. Keep both if you write your own
`Dockerfile`; `vuestrata doctor` warns when the flag is missing. `--check`
ignores it: what is committed is always the narrow form.

### `vp dev` and `vp preview` enforce the policy

Both servers send the generated policy as a `Content-Security-Policy` header,
enforced. An origin missing from `deploy.config.ts` is therefore blocked, and
reported in the console, while you are writing the code that calls it, rather
than in the first deployment that sends headers.

- **`vp preview`** sends exactly what a deployment would, for the environment it
  is started in: `VUESTRATA_API_URL` and the variables named under
  `connectSrcFromEnv` / `websocketFromEnv`. The page is the one the build wrote.
- **`vp dev`** adds one source, the WebSocket of its own hot-update channel,
  and renders the page's `<meta>` for the same environment, so a cross-origin
  `VUESTRATA_API_URL` works without regenerating anything.

One response is sent without the header in both: `/mockServiceWorker.js`. A
service worker is governed by the policy its own script was served with, and
the demo's worker re-fetches what it has no handler for, web fonts included;
under `connect-src 'self'` it would block them. A production build has no
worker.

## The Docker image

The `Dockerfile` builds the production bundle and serves it with unprivileged
nginx on port 8080, for `linux/amd64` and `linux/arm64`:

```bash
docker build -t acme-console .
docker buildx build --platform linux/arm64 -t acme-console .   # e.g. for Graviton
```

A build for a platform other than the host's runs under emulation, which is
slow. An arm64 machine such as Apple Silicon or Graviton builds arm64 natively.

**Route `/api` in front of the container.** The image serves the app, not your
API. With a same-origin `VUESTRATA_API_URL` such as the default `/api`, the
ingress or reverse proxy in front of the container must send `/api/` to your
backend. When nothing does, the container answers `/api` and `/api/*` with a `502` and a
JSON body, `{"error":"api_not_routed", …}`, rather than with the app's
`index.html`, so the missing route is reported as what it is. An absolute
`VUESTRATA_API_URL` needs no route and gets no such block. Which of the two
applies is decided when the container starts, from the URL it is started with.

**Probe `/healthz`.** nginx answers `GET /healthz` itself, with `200 ok`: never
cached, never written to the access log. The image's `HEALTHCHECK` uses it, and
so should your liveness and readiness probes.

**Compression.** Text assets are gzipped once, at build time, and `gzip_static`
serves those files as they are; other text responses are compressed on the fly.

**Caching.** Only content-hashed files are cached for good:

| Path                                                   | `Cache-Control`                       |
| ------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------- |
| `/assets/*`                                            | `public, max-age=31536000, immutable` |
| `/index.html`, and so every SPA route                  | `no-cache`                            |
| `/version.json`, `/runtime-config.js`                  | `no-store`                            |
| Any other file: favicon, `robots.txt`, manifest, image | `public, max-age=3600`                |

A script, stylesheet, image or font that does not exist is a `404`, not the app:
through the SPA fallback a stale image link would get `index.html` with a `200`,
and nothing would look broken. Error responses carry no cache lifetime.

`vercel.json` and `public/_headers` carry the same rules except the last one.
Those hosts match headers on the request path, and a pattern broad enough for
every other file also covers every SPA route, so there those files keep the
host's default, which revalidates on each request.

## Build once, deploy many

The image is not tied to an environment. Build it once, with the mode and the
adapter, and start that same image wherever it is promoted to:

```bash
docker build -t registry.yourcompany.com/acme-console:$GIT_SHA .

# staging
docker run -e VUESTRATA_API_URL=https://api.staging.yourcompany.com … acme-console:$GIT_SHA
# production: the same image
docker run -e VUESTRATA_API_URL=https://api.yourcompany.com … acme-console:$GIT_SHA
```

### What a container may be started with

| Variable                                                    | Effect at start                                                                 |
| ----------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `VUESTRATA_API_URL`                                         | The app's API base. Its origin joins `connect-src`, or its path gets the `502`. |
| `VUESTRATA_APP_TITLE`                                       | Document title. May hold spaces.                                                |
| `VUESTRATA_SESSION_PERSISTENCE`                             | `none` \| `refresh-cookie` \| `session` \| `local`, and nothing else.           |
| `VUESTRATA_ERROR_REPORTING_DSN`                             | Where errors are reported.                                                      |
| `VUESTRATA_RELEASE`                                         | Version attached to error reports.                                              |
| your variables under `runtime` in `deploy.config.ts`        | Available as `appEnv.…` in the app.                                             |
| any variable under `connectSrcFromEnv` / `websocketFromEnv` | Its origin joins `connect-src`.                                                 |

A variable that is not set, or is set to nothing (`-e VUESTRATA_API_URL=`, a
Helm `value: ""`), keeps the value the image was built with, in the app and in
the headers alike. Anything else in the container's environment is ignored: the
list is generated into `docker/runtime/keys`, and the entrypoint reads nothing
that is not on it. The mode and the auth adapter are not on it and cannot be:
they decide what is in the bundle.

What follows from how this works:

- **A value may hold only URL-safe characters**: letters, digits and
  `-_.~:/?#@&+,=%`, and no more than 2048 of them. These values are written into
  a JavaScript file and an nginx configuration, where a quote, a semicolon, a
  space or a newline would mean something. So the container **refuses to
  start** on any other character, and says which variable.
- **The title may also hold spaces**: `-e VUESTRATA_APP_TITLE="Acme Console"`.
  It is written to `runtime-config.js` and to nothing nginx reads. Quotes,
  `<`, `>` and non-ASCII characters are still refused; set a title that needs
  them as a build argument, where it is inlined rather than written to a file.
- **`VUESTRATA_SESSION_PERSISTENCE` must be one of its four values.** `Session`
  stops the container with the list, where the app alone would only log a
  warning.
- **An API URL on `localhost` is taken as given.** A build refuses a
  placeholder host, because a build pointing there was never configured. A
  container started with `-e VUESTRATA_API_URL=http://localhost:8000` was told
  so on purpose: the app calls that URL and the CSP allows it.
- **A same-origin API path must be its own.** `/assets`, `/healthz`,
  `/index.html`, `/version.json`, `/runtime-config.js` and
  `/mockServiceWorker.js` are answered by the server itself and are refused, as
  is a path with a `.` or `..` segment.
- **A variable named under `connectSrcFromEnv` must be in the container's
  environment.** A value given only as a build argument is in the bundle, where
  the entrypoint cannot see it, and its origin would be missing from the CSP.
  `VUESTRATA_API_URL` is the one exception: the image records the URL it was
  built with and falls back to it.
- **A host must be a plain DNS name or an IPv4 address**, and a port a number
  from 1 to 65535. An IPv6 literal, a wildcard or an internationalised name is
  refused; use the punycode form.
- **`VUESTRATA_RELEASE` set at start changes error reports, not
  `/version.json`.** That file is stamped when the image is built and keeps the
  build's release. It names the build that is running; the variable names what
  you want reports filed under. Set the release as a build argument when the
  two should agree.

### What happens at start

The nginx image runs `docker/entrypoint.d/40-vuestrata-runtime.sh` before it
starts the server. The script writes three files to `/tmp/vuestrata`:

| File                    | Holds                                                            |
| ----------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `runtime-config.js`     | The values above, served at `/runtime-config.js` with `no-store` |
| `security-headers.conf` | The header set, `connect-src` completed for this environment     |
| `api-location.conf`     | The JSON `502` for a same-origin API path, or nothing            |

The server configuration includes the last two, so a container in which the
script did not run has no headers to serve and **does not start**. There is no
way to serve the app without them. A custom `ENTRYPOINT`, or a command other
than `nginx`, skips the script; keep the image's own.

::alert{type="warning"}
**`/tmp/vuestrata` is configuration, not scratch space.** nginx reads two of
those files as server configuration, and the third is the script that tells the
app which API to call. Whoever can write there decides both. Give the container
a `/tmp` of its own (a `tmpfs`, or an `emptyDir` mounted into this container
only) and never mount that volume into a sidecar or another container.
::

### A read-only root filesystem

The container writes to `/tmp` and nowhere else: nginx keeps its pid and
temporary files there, and the entrypoint renders into `/tmp/vuestrata`. Give it
a writable `/tmp` and the rest can be read-only:

```bash
docker run --read-only --tmpfs /tmp -p 8080:8080 \
  -e VUESTRATA_API_URL=https://api.yourcompany.com \
  acme-console:$GIT_SHA
```

`docker-compose.yml` does exactly that. It reads the container's values from
`docker.env`, an optional file of its own: copy `docker.env.example` and set
what differs from the build. It does **not** read them from `.env`, which is
the file Vite uses for development: a localhost API URL there would otherwise
configure the production container.

### Kubernetes

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: acme-console
data:
  VUESTRATA_API_URL: https://api.yourcompany.com
  VUESTRATA_APP_TITLE: Acme Console
  VUESTRATA_SESSION_PERSISTENCE: refresh-cookie
  VUESTRATA_RELEASE: '2f1c9ab'
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: acme-console
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: acme-console }
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: { app: acme-console }
    spec:
      securityContext:
        runAsNonRoot: true
        runAsUser: 101 # the image's nginx user
        seccompProfile: { type: RuntimeDefault }
      containers:
        - name: app
          image: registry.yourcompany.com/acme-console:2f1c9ab
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
          envFrom:
            - configMapRef: { name: acme-console }
          securityContext:
            readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
            allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
            capabilities: { drop: [ALL] }
          volumeMounts:
            - { name: tmp, mountPath: /tmp }
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: 8080 }
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: 8080 }
          resources:
            limits: { memory: 128Mi }
      volumes:
        - name: tmp
          emptyDir: {}
```

The same Deployment serves every environment; only the ConfigMap differs. A
changed ConfigMap takes effect when the pods restart, because the values are
read once, at start. A pod whose ConfigMap holds a value the entrypoint refuses
goes into `CrashLoopBackOff`, with the reason in its log:

```
40-vuestrata-runtime.sh: error: VUESTRATA_SESSION_PERSISTENCE must be one of: none refresh-cookie session local (received "Session").
```

None of these values is a secret — each one ends up in the browser — so a
ConfigMap is the right object, not a Secret. The `tmp` volume belongs to this
container alone: see the warning under
[What happens at start](#what-happens-at-start).

### Static hosts

A static host serves files and has no start. It can still set start-time values,
by writing `runtime-config.js` in the deploy step:

```bash
vpr build
cat > dist/runtime-config.js <<'EOF'
window.__VUESTRATA_RUNTIME__ = { VUESTRATA_API_URL: 'https://api.yourcompany.com' }
EOF
```

Its headers, though, are fixed when it is deployed, and so is the page's own CSP
`<meta>`, which a browser enforces as well. Both must allow the origin you
wrote into the file, or the app's calls are blocked. Before the build, either:

- render them for that origin with
  `VUESTRATA_API_URL=https://api.yourcompany.com node scripts/security/sync-headers.mjs --from-env`,
  as described under [Where each origin comes from](#where-each-origin-comes-from),
  so the tag and `_headers` both name it; or
- run `node scripts/security/sync-headers.mjs --runtime-config`, which leaves
  connections to the header alone in the tag, and set the header for each
  environment on the host.

Its SPA fallback must let `/runtime-config.js` through as a file; `vercel.json`
already excludes it from the rewrite.

## What the frontend is not responsible for

This matters more than anything else on this page.

**Frontend RBAC is a UI capability layer.** `can('orders:manage')` decides
whether a button renders. It does not decide whether an order can be modified.
Every permission check in this codebase is a convenience for the user, and every
one of them can be bypassed by anyone willing to open devtools or type a URL.

Your backend must independently authorise **every** request. If the only thing
standing between a viewer and a deleted record is a hidden button, you do not
have authorisation — you have a hidden button.

The same applies to:

- **Validation.** The zod schemas give fast feedback and a shared contract. They
  run in a browser the user controls.
- **Prices and totals.** The order pricing helper exists so the review step
  shows an accurate figure. The server recomputes from the line items and
  ignores any total the client sends.
- **Rate limiting, audit logging, tenancy isolation.** None of these can exist
  in a client.

## Error reporting

No SDK ships with the template — that keeps an error vendor out of the
dependency graph of anyone who does not want one.

1. Set `VUESTRATA_ERROR_REPORTING_DSN`. It can be set per environment, when the
   container starts.
2. Implement `createReporter()` in
   `src/modules/app/plugins/error-reporting.ts`.
3. Allow the reporter's ingest origin in the CSP, or every report is blocked
   with nothing but a console message: add
   `connectSrcFromEnv: ['VUESTRATA_ERROR_REPORTING_DSN']` under `headers` in
   `deploy.config.ts` and run `vpr security:headers`. If your SDK reports to a
   host other than the DSN's, list that origin under `connectSrc` instead.

The reporter receives each error and its context **as they are**.
`SENSITIVE_KEY_PATTERN` redacts what goes through the logger, not what
`reportError()` hands to your reporter, so scrub tokens, passwords and personal
data in `createReporter()` — most SDKs take a `beforeSend`-style hook for it.

Sourcemaps are generated as `hidden` for demo builds and not at all for
production, so `//# sourceMappingURL=` never reaches a client. To symbolicate
error reports, upload the maps to your provider from CI and delete them before
the artifact is published — never serve them.

## Pre-flight

```bash
vp check                                   # types, lint, format
vpr test --run                             # unit, component, integration
node scripts/docs/check-links.mjs          # docs still describe real files

VUESTRATA_RUNTIME_MODE=production \
VUESTRATA_USE_MOCKS=false \
VUESTRATA_AUTH_ADAPTER=jwt \
VUESTRATA_API_URL=https://api.yourcompany.com \
  vpr build

node scripts/build/verify-bundle.mjs --mode=production
E2E_TARGET=preview vpr test:e2e
```

The full checklist is in [Readiness](../9.readiness).
